newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Shell reports profit rise, share split.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Shell reports profit rise, share split.

text.p: Oil giant Royal Dutch/Shell Group reported a 15 percent rise in 1996 profits on Thursday and pleased investors with share splits and bigger-than-expected dividend increases.
Earnings from oil and gas, boosted by higher oil prices and increased production, easily outweighed a substantial fall in profits from its chemicals business, the group said.
Net profit before special items rose to 5.2 billion pounds($8.5 billion) from 4.52 billion, which was largely in line with analysts' expectations.
But final dividends of 22.5 pence per share for Shell Transport and Trading Co Plc and 6.25 guilders ($3.31) for Royal Dutch Petroleum beat most market forecasts.
The group is 60 percent owned by Royal Dutch Petroleum and 40 percent by Shell Transport and Trading Co.
Royal Dutch announced a four-for-one share split, while Shell Transport is to issue two new shares for every one held.

The stock splits and the dividend payouts fuelled shares to 12-month highs in both London and Amsterdam. Shell climbed 30 pence to 1,093, while Royal Dutch advanced 11.70 guilders to 347.50 in late trading.
The Shell Group, whose return on capital has traditionally lagged that of rival British Petroleum Co, reported a rise above 13 percent, narrowing the gap with BP's 15 percent return.
"BP is still over 15 percent, but Shell is beginning to narrow the gap," said David Stedman, head of research at broker Daiwa Europe.
Shell Transport chairman John Jennings, who will retire in June, said the group's 1996 results had set a "rather satisfactory trend".
But pointing to higher profitability of other oil majors he said "there is no cause for complacency".
Jennings will be replaced in July by Mark Moody-Stuart.
To boost results further, Shell is seeking alliances and co-operation pacts, mainly in the downstream business which is suffering from worldwide overcapacity in the refining industry.
Shell said it hopes to sign a letter of intent within the next few weeks on the planned merger of its downstream operations with those of Texaco and Star Enterprise.
In The Hague, group director Steve Miller told a simultaneous news conference that Shell was considering teaming up with another oil firm in Europe in an effort to lift sagging margins.
Back in London, Shell said it was in talks with one or two British supermarket chains to strike a "food and fuels" deal to fight ferocious competition in the UK petrol market.
Shell has already struck up a similar venture in the Netherlands, where leading retailer Ahold is to set up food shops at Shell's filling stations.
Jennings, however, declined to name the chains Shell was in talks with in Britain.
He said that cash-rich Shell, which has some eight to 10 billion dollars free to spend, was scanning the world for potential acquisitions for all its business segments.
But Jennings added it was very hard finding opportunities to buy at acceptable levels.

Shell, which expects its oil and gas production to grow an annual seven percent in the years to 2001, said growing world oil supplies could outweigh increased demand and cause weaker crude prices after surpassingly strong levels last year.
The company added it might consider some localised refinery run cuts after margins eased at the beginning of the year.

Margins in the chemical sector improved slightly in January after falling late last year due to higher feedstock costs and lower selling prices. But Shell expects generally poor trading conditions in the chemicals business to continue throughout 1997. ($1=.6128 Pound) ($1=1.888 Guilder)
